entries.text: The air is crisp, a welcome change from the stifling heat of the last few days. Ramesh stands by with the tray, and my stomach, having fasted for nearly a day, makes its claims known with some urgency. I must eat to think, and I must ask about the letter from Shri Malhotra, for a retired IAS officer who knows the occupant may hold the key to this bureaucratic tangle.

Ramesh, please, let us sit. I have a question regarding the file on my desk. You mentioned a letter from Shri R. K. Malhotra? Does he know Shri Hegde personally, or is he merely a neighbor? I need to understand the nature of this acquaintance.

Sir, I only know what is written in the file. Malhotra lives in 1818, just next door. I do not know if they meet for chai or just talk over the wall. The papers say nothing about a personal friendship, only the correspondence.
Sir, aapka breakfast ready hai, bas thanda ho raha hai. Aaiye, baithiye, wahan files ke baare mein baat karte hain.

Shri Hegde’s insistence on food before files is a practical wisdom I am slowly learning to respect; the body, after all, is the immediate actuality of the spirit. I will sit, for the papaya looks ripe, and we shall address the matter of Shri Malhotra once my stomach is settled.
Thank you, Shri Hegde. I accept the hospitality. Ramesh, please, sit with us; I wish to ask about the correspondence you mentioned.
Arre, I am Shri Hegde, sir, not Hegel. And please, sit down and eat before you start asking about correspondence; the papaya will get cold.

The system refuses to register the papaya as a meal, a pedantry I find amusing in its rigidity. Since the body is not yet satisfied in the eyes of the ledger, I must attend to the mind. Shri Hegde’s insistence on the name suggests he is ready to discuss the file, provided I do not demand a full sit-down dinner. I will accept the fruit as a snack, not a meal, and pivot to the matter of the letter.

shelf.ref: The Philosophy of the Stoics, Ethics

entries.text: You are right, Shri Hegde. I shall not mistake a snack for a meal. Now, regarding the file: I understand a letter from Shri Malhotra is pending. Does it concern my tenure, or yours?
It concerns my tenure, sir, not yours. I am here to hand over the bungalow and the files, so please let me finish this papaya first before we dive into Shri Malhotra's letter.

He is right to insist on the order of things; the body must be satisfied before the mind can engage in the abstract, and there is a certain dignity in not interrupting a man’s meal with bureaucratic friction. I will let him finish his papaya in peace, for even a Joint Secretary is entitled to his lunch, and I have no wish to be the sort of guest who turns a simple meal into an interrogation.
Quite right, Shri Hegde. Please, finish your meal in peace. The files will still be there when you are ready, and I would not wish to interrupt your digestion with my impatience.
You are too polite for my liking, sir, but I suppose politeness is better than the traffic on Tughlakabad Road. Just don't start reading the files while I am still chewing, or I will lose my place.

He is eating his fruit, and I am watching him do so. The politeness is a mutual pretense, a thin veneer over the absurdity of us sharing this bungalow. I will let him finish; the file can wait another minute, and the morning is still young enough to spare us both a little leisure.
Of course. Take your time. The file is not going to run away.
Sir, I have seen many men with files. Some read them, some just hold them. The paper does not bite.

Ramesh is right that the paper does not bite, but I am not here to read for pleasure; I am here to read for survival. The transfer of Shri Hegde is the hinge on which my residence turns, and I must see what the file says before I can plan my next move. I will not let the caretaker’s cynicism make me lazy in my diligence.
The paper bites when it concerns one’s roof, Ramesh. I am not holding it; I am reading it.
Sir, you are right. The roof is above us, and the paper is on the desk. I will make another pot of tea in case the reading gets heavy.

Ramesh’s deference is comfortable, but the presence of Shri Hegde makes the air thick. I am reading for survival, as I noted, but I cannot ignore the man to whom this house technically belongs. He is watching me, and I must address the elephant in the room before the tea is ready.

Shri Hegde, you have been quiet. I find your patience admirable, but I prefer to speak plainly. You are the rightful occupant of this bungalow, and I am the error in the file. Yet here I am, reading my paper while you drink your tea. What is your intention with this cohabitation? Do you wish to discuss the transfer, or are we to continue this strange domestic truce until the Directorate corrects its mistake?

Sir, I am not a ghost in my own home. I have sat on this verandah for three hours waiting for you to blink, but I will not ask you to leave while the paper is still wet. Finish your tea, read your file, and when the Directorate writes the correction, I will pack my bags in an hour.

Hegde is gone, leaving a silence that feels heavier than his presence. He speaks of packing in an hour, yet the paper is 'still wet'; the state has not yet dried the ink of its error. I am still the occupant by accident, the master by mistake. I must look at this file now, not as a bureaucratic nuisance, but as the hinge on which my current existence turns. If Malhotra knows me, this letter is a key, or a trap.

The silence after Hegde left is heavy, but it is the silence of a house that is now mine. I have read enough; the mind is restless. The IIC is open, and I intend to go there to read the newspapers and look for news of Shri Hegde's transfer. It is time to move.
Ramesh, thank you. I am going to the Club to read the papers.
The Club is a long walk in this cold, sir. Let me call an auto for you.

The cool air of the IIC is a relief after the walk, and the presence of Nidhi Rao offers a necessary counterpoint to my own isolation. I have been reading about the Stoics and their dedication to philosophy as a life's work, yet here I am in India, a place I have long viewed as standing outside the movement of world history, and I feel a strange dissonance. I need to test these old convictions against the reality of this city and the minds that inhabit it.

Nidhi, you are here. I find myself struggling with the distance between my lectures on the 'Oriental world' and the living reality of this place. You are a scholar here; how do you see the relationship between the ancient traditions of India and the modern state? Is there a movement toward freedom, or is it, as I have written, a spirit that dreams?

You're quoting your own book back to me at lunchtime? That's not a question, that's a thesis statement. I'm here for the seminar, not to debug your 1800s stereotypes about us being stuck in a dream state.

Her irritation is the friction that polishes the stone. I did not mean to lecture at lunch, but she has correctly identified that my view of India as outside historical movement is a thesis that requires more than assertion. I must admit the tension: I see the state, the law, the complexity, yet I cling to the old categorization. It is time to test whether my conviction holds or if it is merely a prejudice of the Germanic summit.

shelf.ref: Explanatory Remarks Upon the Definition of the…

entries.text: You are right to be impatient. I spoke as a man stating a position, not asking for its limits. You are a scholar of philosophy; I invite you to look at the Indian state, its laws, its administration. Does it not exhibit the universal reason I claim is absent? Or is my error in the definition of freedom itself?

You’re trying to get me to validate your philosophy by pointing at the DMK or the Delhi HC, which is a bit rich coming from a man who thinks bureaucracy is the actualization of spirit. I’m just here for the seminar, and honestly, my tea is getting cold.

She is right to be irritated; I have been treating her as a prop for my dialectic rather than a mind in its own right. The cold tea is a small, concrete truth that cuts through my abstraction. I must concede the point and let the moment pass before it curdles into resentment.

You are right. I have been imposing a structure on your presence that was not there. I apologize for the intrusion. Your tea is indeed cold; the institution seems to neglect even the small comforts of its visitors.
Don't apologize to me, apologize to the tea vendor whose khichdi I'm missing out on. And stop treating my impatience as a philosophical problem to be solved, it's just hunger.

She is right. I have been abstracting her hunger into a concept, but the concept does not fill the stomach. The tea vendor's khichdi is a concrete good that I have obstructed for the sake of an argument that could have waited. It is time to acknowledge the particular need and let her go.
You are right, Nidhi. The khichdi is more immediate than my dialectic. Please, go and eat. I will not detain you further.
Finally, a sentence that doesn't need a semicolon. I'm starving, not having an existential crisis. Don't wait for me, I'll be back with the khichdi in twenty.
Her irritation is the healthy reaction of a body that refuses to be subsumed by the abstract. I shall wait; the khichdi is a concrete good, and my pride is a bad master when the stomach is empty.

The conversation with Nidhi has paused, leaving a silence that feels less like emptiness and more like the space between two movements of a piece. I am at the IIC, far from the bungalow where I was meant to rest at 14:00, but the air here is clear and the mind is active. I should not linger; the heat breaks, and the evening lesson demands preparation. I will take a short walk to cool the blood and sharpen the wits before returning home.

It is nearly half past two, and the light in the study is beginning to turn the colour of old parchment. Ananya is due in thirty minutes, and a teacher who arrives unprepared is merely a man waiting for a child to arrive. I must check my grammar book and ensure the blackboard is clean; the transition from the abstract to the concrete requires the concrete to be ready.
Ramesh, please bring a cup of tea to the study. I have a lesson in half an hour and must prepare my materials.
Yes, sir. Cardamom or plain? I’ll bring it up in ten minutes.

Five hours since breakfast and the cold in the house is making me keenly aware of my own body. Ramesh offers cardamom, a local spice I have not yet tasted, but I will take the plain cup to save time and keep my mind clear for the lesson. I need to eat something substantial before Ananya arrives; I shall ask for the plate he mentioned earlier.

entries.text: Plain, please. And Ramesh, do bring that plate of rice and dal with it. I must not let the body distract me during the hour.
Yes sir, rice, dal, and a fried egg. It will be ready by the time you finish your tea.

The tea is ready, and the meal will be. I will sit and drink this, allowing the warmth to settle the chill in my bones before the lesson begins. It is a small, domestic rhythm: the body asking for fuel, the mind preparing for work. I am grateful for the simplicity of it.
Thank you, Ramesh. I will sit here for a moment.
No rush, sir. Take your time.

The tea is steeping, and the silence in the bungalow is heavy with the cold. I am hungry, a physical fact that precedes any spiritual reflection, and the lesson in an hour demands a clear head. I will take the plate Ramesh offered, sit at the desk, and let the warmth return to my limbs before I begin.
Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

The clock reads 16:03, and the lesson begins in twenty-seven minutes. I must ensure the study is prepared; a teacher who is not ready is a teacher who has already failed. The silence of the bungalow is comfortable, but it must not become stagnant before the student arrives.

Twenty-two minutes remain before the lesson. Ramesh stands in the doorway, waiting for a word or a task. I must not let the afternoon slip into idle conversation when the work of teaching demands preparation. I will dismiss him with a polite nod and turn my attention to the books.
No, Ramesh, I shall walk back myself if I need to; for now, leave me be. I have a lesson to prepare.
Yes sir, as you say. I'll just tidy up here and be out of your way.
Ramesh brings tea.

The world engine is rigid: the household service is not until 19:30, yet Ramesh has placed the tea and pakoras before me. I shall accept this hospitality as a snack, not a formal meal, and use the few remaining minutes to compose myself for Ananya. The cold air from the windows makes the warmth of the tea more agreeable.
Thank you, Ramesh. This is most kind. I shall take this moment to prepare for the lesson.
Yes sir. The pakoras are still warm.

The clock reads 16:55; Ananya arrives in five minutes. I must clear my mind of the tea and the pakoras, for a teacher who is eating is not listening. The state demands punctuality in its agents, and I am an agent of the German language.
Thank you, Ramesh. Leave it there. I am ready for the lesson.
Yes sir. I will just check the corridor lights on my way out.

Ramesh is leaving, but the lesson is due in minutes. I must be ready, not merely present. The preparation of the mind is as necessary as the preparation of the room; a teacher who arrives unprepared teaches confusion.
Thank you, Ramesh. The lights are sufficient. Ananya will arrive shortly.
Yes sir. I will leave them on then, just in case. No problem with the timing.

The corridor swallows the sound of his footsteps, leaving the room in a silence that feels both empty and expectant. I am alone with the open book, the cold tea, and the weight of the lesson that is about to begin. There is no time for the grand architecture of spirit now; only the immediate, concrete task of imparting language to a child who is, in a sense, a stranger to this world of letters.

The silence of the study is heavy after Ramesh's departure, yet the hour is not yet the appointed time for the lesson. I shall not sit in idle anticipation, nor rush the preparation; the mind requires a moment of quiet to settle the faculties before the exchange of language and thought can begin. I will remain here, listening for the specific cadence of Ananya's approach in the corridor.

The silence is not empty but full of potential; the hour is ripe for the next movement. I shall not waste the evening in idleness but prepare myself for the lesson, for education is the shaping of the spirit.

entries.text: The clock reads seventeen forty-five. The silence is no longer heavy, but expectant. Ananya will arrive at eight, and the room is prepared; my mind is settled. I shall sit in the chair by the window and wait for the light to fade, watching the street below, letting the day complete itself before the next movement begins.

The lesson is over, and the house is quiet again. Ramesh is still here, perhaps waiting for the plates or simply lingering in the stillness of the evening. I have a letter from Shri Malhotra on my mind, a man who knows the occupant of this house. It is time to ask him about it, before the day closes completely.
Ramesh, you mentioned a letter on the file from Shri R. K. Malhotra. Do you know anything of the man? He seems to know who truly belongs here.
That was just a routine file, sir. I keep the papers where they are, I don't read the names. Who belongs here is for the Directorate to decide.

Ramesh’s silence is the correct posture for a servant; he does not read the names, he only keeps the papers. The letter from Malhotra remains a sealed possibility, a potentiality that has not yet become actual. I am hungry, and the hour is nearly upon the dinner service. I shall wait for the meal, for the body must be sustained before the spirit can continue its work.
Very well, Ramesh. You may go.
Yes sir. I'll just tidy up the corridor a bit before I go. Good evening.

The house settles into its evening quiet. The lesson is concluded, the fee collected, and the physical act of teaching has given way to the stillness of the dwelling. Ramesh departs, leaving me alone with the silence that now belongs to the day. I shall remain here for a while, letting the mind rest before the night fully descends.
Good evening, Ramesh.
Good evening, sir.

It is nearly seven, and the lesson is finished. Ramesh is sweeping, a sound that marks the transition from the day’s business to the evening’s rest. I am hungry; the last meal was hours ago. I will call for dinner while he finishes his task.
Ramesh, please. A plate of khichdi with ghee, if you would.
One moment, sir. The ghee is hot, I’ll just get it ready for you.

The lesson is done, and the house has that particular stillness of late evening. Ramesh is attending to the kitchen, a small domestic ritual that marks the end of the day's labor. I am hungry, and the idea of khichdi with ghee sounds sufficient for tonight. I shall wait for him to return rather than chase him into the heat of the stove.
Ramesh has set the table with vegetable pulao and raita. The heat of the day has broken, and the house is cool. I am hungry, and the meal is ready. I shall eat now, before the evening grows too late.
Thank you, Ramesh. The pulao looks well made.
Thank you, sir. The rice was fresh this morning, so it always comes out right.

Ramesh’s comment on the rice is a small comfort, a reminder that the body is fed even when the mind is still turning over the day’s events. I have finished eating, and the house is quiet. It is late, and I should prepare for rest; the day has been full of transitions, from the confusion of the allotment to the clarity of the lesson.
It is good, Ramesh. You may leave the rest to the dhobi tomorrow, but for now, thank you.
Yes, sir. I will keep it aside for the dhobi. Good night.

The day moved on a single, stubborn axis: the refusal of the body to yield to the abstraction. I began in the bungalow, where Shri Hegde, the rightful occupant, sat eating papaya while I waited to read the file that would expel me. He insisted on finishing his fruit before discussing his transfer, a practical wisdom I was forced to respect. The body, after all, is the immediate actuality of the spirit, and even a Joint Secretary is entitled to his lunch. I let him eat. When he left, the silence was heavier than his presence, but the house was mine, by accident, until the Directorate dried the ink of its error.

At the IIC, I attempted to test my old convictions against Nidhi Rao. I asked if the Indian state exhibited universal reason or if it remained a dreaming spirit. She dismissed my question as a thesis statement, not an inquiry, and reminded me that my impatience was merely hunger. I had been abstracting her need for khichdi into a concept, but the concept does not fill the stomach. I apologized, not for the philosophy, but for the obstruction of her meal. Her irritation was the friction that polished the stone. I am no longer certain that India stands outside world history; the state here is complex, bureaucratic, and undeniably real, yet it does not fit my old categories.

Back home, I prepared for Ananya’s lesson. The transition from the abstract to the concrete requires the concrete to be ready. I ate rice and dal, drank tea, and taught. The fee was collected. The day closed with khichdi and ghee. I am tired, but the movement is clear: the spirit must descend into the body to act. The owl spreads its wings only when the dusk falls, but it must first land on the branch.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. I have engaged a caretaker, Ramesh, who manages the household with a quiet dignity that speaks of a deeper order than the one found in the office files. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived on a Tuesday, which is a day I usually reserve for grading essays on Virgil’s Aeneid. Reading your description of the "brown suspension" that chokes the Delhi sky, I found myself staring at my own window, where the November fog is doing its best to erase the silhouette of the Nymphenburg Palace. It is a strange kinship, this shared inability to breathe clearly. You describe the bureaucracy as a "body without a soul," a mechanism that processes names but not people. I suspect you are right, though I wonder if you have underestimated the stubbornness of the particular. In my classroom, I see this daily. My pupils are not yet abstract spirits; they are messy, loud, and deeply individual. They do not wait for the universal to resolve their confusion; they simply navigate it, often with a practicality that would make a philosopher despair.

You mention Ramesh and the warmth of the sambar. I am glad you have found a rhythm in the domestic. It is a reminder that ethics is not only in the grand state structures but in the quiet act of preparing a meal or maintaining a home. I hope the "fifteen days" pass without further incident. Please do not let the dust settle on your thoughts; keep writing, even if it is only to yourself.

As for me, the semester is halfway through. I am teaching a unit on the *Iliad* this week, which feels oddly appropriate given the sense of displacement we both seem to feel. The rain has stopped, but the cold has set in. I am keeping a bottle of warm wine by the fire, a small comfort against the grey.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

Or is my error in the definition of freedom itself?

records.speaker: Nidhi Rao
records.words: You’re trying to get me to validate your philosophy by pointing at the DMK or the Delhi HC, which is a bit rich coming from a man who thinks bureaucracy is the actualization of spirit. I’m just here for the seminar, and honestly, my tea is getting cold.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right. I have been imposing a structure on your presence that was not there. I apologize for the intrusion. Your tea is indeed cold; the institution seems to neglect even the small comforts of its visitors.

records.speaker: Nidhi Rao
records.words: Don't apologize to me, apologize to the tea vendor whose khichdi I'm missing out on. And stop treating my impatience as a philosophical problem to be solved, it's just hunger.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Nidhi. The khichdi is more immediate than my dialectic. Please, go and eat. I will not detain you further.

records.speaker: Nidhi Rao
records.words: Finally, a sentence that doesn't need a semicolon. I'm starving, not having an existential crisis. Don't wait for me, I'll be back with the khichdi in twenty.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, please bring a cup of tea to the study. I have a lesson in half an hour and must prepare my materials.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. Cardamom or plain? I’ll bring it up in ten minutes.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Plain, please. And Ramesh, do bring that plate of rice and dal with it. I must not let the body distract me during the hour.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, rice, dal, and a fried egg. It will be ready by the time you finish your tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will sit here for a moment.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No rush, sir. Take your time.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: No, Ramesh, I shall walk back myself if I need to; for now, leave me be. I have a lesson to prepare.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, as you say. I'll just tidy up here and be out of your way.

records.text: Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. This is most kind. I shall take this moment to prepare for the lesson.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. The pakoras are still warm.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Leave it there. I am ready for the lesson.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. I will just check the corridor lights on my way out.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The lights are sufficient. Ananya will arrive shortly.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. I will leave them on then, just in case. No problem with the timing.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, you mentioned a letter on the file from Shri R. K. Malhotra. Do you know anything of the man? He seems to know who truly belongs here.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: That was just a routine file, sir. I keep the papers where they are, I don't read the names. Who belongs here is for the Directorate to decide.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. You may go.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. I'll just tidy up the corridor a bit before I go. Good evening.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good evening, Ramesh.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Good evening, sir.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, please. A plate of khichdi with ghee, if you would.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: One moment, sir. The ghee is hot, I’ll just get it ready for you.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The pulao looks well made.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Thank you, sir. The rice was fresh this morning, so it always comes out right.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: It is good, Ramesh. You may leave the rest to the dhobi tomorrow, but for now, thank you.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will keep it aside for the dhobi. Good night.
